slots.text: Most founders validate ideas by asking "would you use this?" Wrong question. Ask "how are you solving this problem today?" Then sit quietly while they walk through their current painful workflow.

Signs your user interview went well:
1. They asked when it'll be ready
2. They offered to introduce you to their colleague
3. They described their current solution as "a total mess"
4. The call ran 20 minutes over

AI tools create this weird paradox for founders. They make building faster but validation slower. You can prototype in days now, but that just means you're more attached to the wrong solution when users finally tell you it sucks.
Teams that obsess over removing one click from their workflow will simultaneously make users fill out 12-field signup forms. The friction you see isn't always the friction that matters.
"Talk to users" is startup gospel but nobody mentions the part where users lie to you. Not maliciously. They just can't predict their own behavior. Watch what they do, not what they say they'll do.

Workflow friction usually hides in:
1. Handoffs between tools
2. Manual data entry they've accepted as "just how it is"
3. Things they do "just to be safe"
4. Processes that made sense 2 years ago but nobody questions
Most founders ask users what they want instead of watching what they actually do. The gap between those two things is where most products die.

Three ways user interviews go wrong:

1. You ask leading questions that confirm your bias
2. You talk to people who will never pay for anything
3. You mistake politeness for genuine interest

All fixable, but takes practice.

The hardest part about building with AI isn't the technical stuff. It's figuring out which manual tasks are actually worth automating. Most workflows exist for reasons you don't see until you try to remove them.
Founders who validate ideas by building prototypes skip faster than founders who validate with landing pages or interviews. Less emotional attachment to code they haven't written yet.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes the steps you want to eliminate are the ones that make users think twice about decisions they shouldn't rush.
You can't validate a business idea without talking to strangers. But most technical founders would rather build for six months than have ten awkward conversations. The math on this is brutal.
Most founders ask users what they want instead of watching what they actually do. The gap between stated preferences and behavior is where real insights live.

Three things that kill user interviews:
1. Leading questions that validate your assumptions
2. Talking more than listening
3. Asking about hypothetical future behavior instead of past actions

The hardest part about building with AI isn't the tech—it's figuring out which manual processes are actually worth automating. Half the workflows people complain about exist for good reasons they forgot.
Founders who ship fast tend to use boring, proven tools. Founders who spend months choosing the perfect stack tend to ship slowly. The correlation is stronger than I expected.
Friction in workflows is like pain in your body. Sometimes it signals real problems that need fixing. Sometimes it's just the cost of doing something worthwhile.

Signs your idea validation is actually just confirmation bias:
1. You only talk to people who already agree with you
2. You dismiss negative feedback as 'not getting it'
3. You haven't changed anything based on user input
Most founders treat user interviews like feature requests sessions. Wrong game. You're mining for jobs-to-be-done, not building a wishlist.

Signs your idea validation is actually just confirmation bias:

1. Only talking to people who already love you
2. Leading questions that beg for yes
3. Skipping the "would you pay" conversation
4. Cherry-picking feedback that fits

The AI tooling space is getting weird. Everyone's building the same workflow automations but calling them different things. Starting to think the real opportunity is in the boring, unsexy processes nobody talks about.
Founders who say "we'll figure out monetization later" usually mean "we're afraid to test if anyone will actually pay for this."
Removing friction sounds simple until you realize most friction exists because someone else optimized for their workflow, not yours.

What actually kills early-stage momentum:

1. Building features users mention but don't use
2. Optimizing the wrong metrics
3. Talking to users who aren't your customers
4. Solving problems that aren't painful enough
Most founders skip validation because they're afraid of hearing 'no.' But the real fear should be building something nobody wants for 18 months.

3 signs you're talking to the wrong users:
1. They love everything about your idea
2. They can't tell you the last time they had this problem
3. They keep suggesting features for 'other people'
The hardest part about building with AI isn't the tech stack or the prompts. It's knowing when to stop tweaking and ship something that's 'good enough' when the model could theoretically be better.
Founders who obsess over removing friction from their product often create the most friction in their sales process. Seven discovery calls to buy a $49/month tool.
User interviews where you ask 'Would you use this?' are worthless. Ask 'Walk me through the last time you dealt with this problem' instead.

4 workflow friction points I see everywhere:
1. Too many approval layers
2. Context switching between tools
3. Manual data entry that could be automated
4. Notifications that train people to ignore them
Most founders skip validation because they're afraid of hearing 'no.' But 100 nos from strangers beats one yes from your mom when you're trying to build something people actually want.

Three signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They love everything you show them
2. They ask when it'll be free
3. They keep suggesting features for other people

Find the ones with the problem, not the ones being polite.
AI tools make it easier to build the wrong thing faster. Founders are shipping MVPs in days now, but still taking months to figure out if anyone cares.

The workflow friction that kills startups isn't technical debt. It's the mental overhead of switching between 12 different tools just to answer 'are we building something people want?' Most teams spend more time managing their stack than talking to users.
User interviews are not about asking people what they want. They're about understanding what they're already doing badly and how much that bothers them.

Four workflow killers I see in every early team:

1. Slack threads that should be docs
2. Daily standups about yesterday's blockers
3. Feature requests from users who don't pay
4. Building before you know what success looks like

3 things that kill idea validation:

1. Asking what people want instead of watching what they do
2. Talking to people who are too polite to tell you the truth
3. Validating the idea you want to build, not the problem that exists
User interviews where everyone says "that's interesting" are worthless. You want people who either get angry about the problem or completely dismiss your solution.

The hardest part about building with AI isn't the tech - it's that users expect magic but can't articulate what magic looks like. So you build something technically impressive that solves a problem they didn't know they had.
Most workflow friction comes from switching contexts, not from individual tools being slow. People will use terrible software if it keeps them in the same mental space.

Signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They have all day to chat with you
2. They love talking about their problems but never mention solutions they've tried
3. They want to give you feature requests before understanding what you're building
The best validation happens when someone interrupts your pitch to ask how much it costs and when they can start using it.
